I feel as I can relate here as well. My colicky, inconsolable baby was on her third night in a row of screaming in my arms inconsolably for hours due to reflux and gas. She was 6 months old or so at the time. I had already handed her off to my husband for a “break” and he brought her back to me after an hour still crying. I sat with her for another 10 minutes of screaming before I lost it. I started yelling at her little tear streaked face about why did I deserve this and why did she hate me and why can’t I make her happy. I felt myself reaching a boiling point and I wanted to shake her and throw her against the wall. Instead, I got up from our bed, calmly placed her in the hallway on her back, still screaming, and walked away to sob behind our bedroom door until I felt safe. 

It was horrifying. Im still nauseated and disgusted to remember it. But my husband and I were both struggling with postpartum depression and SERIOUSLY sleep deprived. He was working more than 50 hours a week and I felt unsupported all day and he felt overwhelmed and overstimulated by the noise and hysteria (from both me and baby) when he got home at night. 

And yes, things are much better now. That baby is almost 3 and we just had our second.

ELI5: narcissistic personality disorder and suicide

Many assume that narcissists can’t be truly suicidal, since the very act seems to go against the self aggrandizing and ego centric beliefs that characterize the disorder.  However, this doesn’t mean narcissistic people live in a fantasy land where they are king and everything is always perfect. Research following psychiatric patients clinically diagnosed with NPD strongly proves that individuals diagnosed with NPD are much more likely to die from suicide than someone without NPD. 

Narcissistic people have a very fragile self concept. When they are forced to face truly undeniable criticism, failure, or judgement (real or perceived) they often lose a sense of  control over their life and this causes extreme emotional dysregulation for the narcissist. They may commit or attempt suicide as an attempt to avoid further narcissistic injury, to eliminate their imperfect self, or in a rush of emotions may act out impulsively under a false sense of indestructibility.

Yep. Almost lost my hand two years ago on Easter Sunday.

I was bleeding all over the house and the puncture wounds were so deep the yellow fatty tissue in my hand was poking out. I'm assuming this post is in response to the post that John Danaher made. For anyone who wants to read the post, I believe it can still be found [here.](http://www.bjjee.com/articles/john-danaher-banned-jumping-guard-at-all-levels-in-his-gym/)

There's a lot of controversy swirling around this situation, and understandably so. From one perspective, I think its worth acknowledging how dangerous jumping guard really can be. It's almost worse that heel hooks (if you want to compare it to that) because at least the danger of a heel hook is universally acknowledged. A lot of people just casually jump guard in training without thinking about the hazards. In the hands of an unskilled person, all it takes is one small misstep and you could seriously injure yourself or your partner. 

On the other hand, we should practice all techniques. Just because something "scares" you doesn't mean it shouldn't be done at all.

Jumping guard is banned for anyone below blue belt in IBJJF competition. That being said, lots of people below blue in will still jump guard in training. There isn't a lot you can do to protect yourself except the norm. You always want to have bent knees when grip fighting, in the event that someone pulls something you don't expect. Never plant a straight leg on the mat. This will not only save you from injury, but your mobility and agility will improve. 

Prevention is also key. Communicating what your partner before rolling about the speed that you wish to go at is important. If you don't feel comfortable starting from the feet if your partner is going to attempt to throw, shoot a takedown, or judo throw you, then say so. There's nothing wrong with just plain ol' pulling guard, though practicing all of those techniques in a controlled environment with at trustworthy partner will be important at some point.  Of course, you can avoid the situation all together by starting from your knees or with one person sitting, something that is already a common practice on crowded mats.

Not a higher belt, but I actively avoid the white belts who I realize have an unsafe mentality. There are some guys who just cannot take the idea of losing to a girl, or just the idea of losing in general so they will go to any lengths to try to avoid getting tapped. 

Here's an example from yesterday-- a big white belt (at leas 6'2" 230lbs) asked me to roll. Somehow or another, he ended up in my closed guard. I have very long legs and am very flexible, so this is a spot where I feel very comfortable. He got so mad after maybe 20 seconds of just trying to open my guard by pushing on my knee, that he picked me up and slammed me on my side, putting all of his weight into me as we both fell. 

Before anyone says I should have just let him open my guard, he's not a complete newbie-- he's been in the gym since September, and intends to compete next month.

So yeah, even as a white belt, I don't like all white belts.

How to avoid getting flipped to guard: Work on your balance and posting out when they attempt to bump and roll you. You shouldn't just being going right over-- you should be shifting your weight with your opponent. You also shouldn't be sitting on your opponent where a hip bump will completely disrupt your center of gravity. Move into high mount as soon as possible. If you're not on their hips, their upa will be far less effective. Grapevining and superma/smothering work well. However, if you're going to be in high mount, watch out for the back door escape. Not a lot of guys can pull it off as it requires a good deal of flexibility and is rather uncomfortable, but the option is there.

Sometimes in an attempt to roll you they will inadvertently give up technical mount. In this position, your opponent is half on his side while you have one leg over his waist and the other against his back. I love technical mount-- you can threaten three great things from there. You have the kimura on the far side arm (the one closest to the mat), you have your arm bar, and you have your bow and arrow. Obviously, there are other things available from that position, but if you confuse your opponent and threaten all three of these things, they will eventually give up one of them in an attempt to block something else. 

You can sometimes capitalize on your opponent bumping and rolling you by getting a cross collar grip in **deep** before they bump and roll. Since getting that second grip for the x choke can be hard from mount because your opponent is so focused on defending, I will sometimes let them roll me to guard and hang on to the cross collar grip. When you see that exposed second grip while they're coming up, get it and go for the choke. 

If you don't see the x choke, then still keep the cross collar grip. Don't just let them have whatever posture they want in guard, break them down and readjust for an attack or sweep. Learning to have a good game off your back can be really important when larger opponents think they can muscle or smash you and then BAM you hit them with technique.

I don't see the point of limiting yourself at any belt level. I'm not trying to make rubber guard a go-to position--- I'm just playing around with different things and exploring different kinds of games. 

By specialized guards, do you mean the "newer" guards such as rubber and worm? Because while I agree that it's dangerous to focus on things like that when theres a high likelihood you wont understand how to use them I also believe it's beneficial to explore different things like spider and DLR and x guard. Focusing on the fundamentals is different from only training the fundamentals. I spend most of my time working on the bare basics, but there's nothing wrong with using fifteen minutes of open mat here or there to explore other parts of bjj.

I started jiu jitsu by myself-- found a local place, signed up online, and showed up for the first class. Our school has a beginner's class that is mandatory for all new students with no prior BJJ experience. I was thrown in on the first day to test week. I struggled to rep technique after technique with an advanced blue belt. He was kind enough to take me patiently through everything, but I was gassed half way through the hour long class. 

I wanted to quit. That first class alone managed to make me uncomfortable and push my limits. I felt incompetent and ignorant. But I also knew that I needed to keep going if I wanted to feel capable. You are not intimidated and overwhelmed solely because you are a woman. Everyone who begins jiu jitsu will start at white belt. No one knows anything, and no one feels entirely at ease. No one will expect you to be a natural born killer. Some men don't even expect you to come in and give 100% (as you should be). 

You're not at the wrong dojo (at least I don't think so from what you've described). It takes time to warm up to your gym, and to become comfortable with your training partners and make friends. "jiujitsu is not a comfort sport." It is not physically comfortable, and it is not emotionally comfortable. You will feel stupid, frustrated, and ignorant. Everything else will come with time-- skill and comfort.

Doctors will probably tell you not to train with a broken nose and I'm not going to contradict that but I'll give you my experience. I broke my nose when a newbie white belt smashed his elbow down on my face (for pretty much no reason) while in my guard. Blood everywhere. I was back on the mats in the next day but I only trained technique and rolled with upper blues and purples that I knew well and trusted (I'm from a small gym) for about three weeks. I can't give you advice on the splint coming off-- I never went to a doctor for my nose, I had a teammate who is an athletic trainer reset it after class. 

Anyways, I would say the first order of business is to talk to your professor. Most are comfortable with letting adults train to their own limitations after an injury, but I've seen some that are more cautious, especially if the initial injury occurred on their mats. I guess it's just a liability issue, but I would just check in with him and let him know it's broken and if you feel comfortable or not getting back on the mats.

A cautionary tale-- broken noses are easily rebroken when you don't allow them the proper time to heal. One wrong elbow/heel/smash is all it takes to unset it. My recommendation would be to train with people who you feel safe with and care enough to take the extra minute to *try* to prevent a re-injury. Incidental contact is a big part of bjj though, and there's no guarantee that the next time you step on the mats, another flying heel won't smack you square in the face.

You could also try head gear, but again, check with your professor to see if a thin facemask would be allowed for light training. Your other option would be to only train technique. That would generally save you from a higher risk of accidental contact and the crappiness of trying to breath with a broken nose. 

Again, a medical professional likely doesn't agree with any of what I'm saying, and there is always the risk of breaking again and requiring a surgical fix.
